Statement 
As per Seventh Schedule of the Constitu tion of India, subjects of Police and 
Public Order are with the State Governments. However, the Government of India 
(GoI) has been supplementing the efforts of  States affected by Left Wing Extremism 
(LWE). To address the LWE problem holistica lly, a "National Policy and Action Plan

to address LWE" was approv ed in 2015. It envisages a multi-pronged strategy 
involving security related measures, development interventions, ensuring rights and 
entitlements of local communities etc.  
(i) On security front, the GoI assists the LWE affected State Government by 
providing Central Armed Police Forces an d raising of India Reserve Battalions, 
helicopter support, strengthening of security  camp infrastructure, training, funds for 
modernization of State police forces, equi pment & arms, sharing of intelligence, 
construction of Fortified Police Stations etc.   
• For capacity building of states since 2014-15, Rs. 3681.73 crore have been 
released to LWE affected states on op erational expenditure and training needs 
of Security Forces, rehabilitation of  surrendered LWE cadre, ex-gratia to 
families of martyred securi ty force personnel/civilians killed in LWE violence 
etc. under Security Related Expenditure (SRE) scheme.  
• GoI and State Governments have form ulated comprehensive surrender-cum-
rehabilitation policies. The GoI also su pports the States in the endeavor 
through ‘Surrender-cum-Rehabilitation’ Policy as part of Security Related 
Expenditure (SRE) Scheme.  The GoI reimburses the expenditure incurred by 
the LWE affected States on rehab ilitation of surrenders under the SRE 
Scheme.  The rehabilitation package inte r-alia, includes an immediate grant of 
Rs. 5 lakhs for higher ranked LWE cadres and Rs 2.5 lakhs for other LWE 
cadres. In addition, incentives for surrender of weapons/ammunition are also 
provided under the Scheme. In addition , provision also exists for imparting 
training in trade/vocation of their liking with monthly stipend of Rs. 10,000/- for 
three years. The affected  States have further revised their Surrender cum 
Rehabilitation policies to make them lucrative and contemporary. 
• The efforts of the States for equipping and modernizing their police forces have 
been supplemented under the scheme of  "Modernization of Police Forces". 
Under the scheme, central assistance is provided to the State Governments for 
weapons, equipment for information technology, communication, training, 
construction of Police Stations, mobility and construction of police housing and 
other police infrastructure etc. Under its sub scheme i.e. Special Infrastructure 
Scheme (SIS), works of Rs. 1761 crore have been sanctioned to LWE affected 
states for strengthening of State’s Special Forces, State Intelligence Branches 
(SIBs), District Police and construction of Fortified Police Stations (FPS). The 
GoI’s focus on security infrastructure has been pivotal. So far 656 fortified 
police stations have been built.

• Under Assistance to Central Agencies  for LWE Management (ACALWEMS) 
Scheme, assistance is provided for basic structure of camps and for 
provisioning of helicopters for counter  LWE operations. Rs1224.59 Crores has 
been provided to Central Agencies through this scheme since 2014-15. 
• There has been a special focus on the financial choking of LWEs and 
unearthing of the nexus be tween CPI (Maoists) and its financial supporters. 
For effective action towards choking of funds and other resources to LWE, 
coordinated actions are being taken by State Police in cooperation with Central 
agencies by various means.Steps being taken by the Government to prevent 
the financing of LWE:- 
 A dedicated structure of "Combating Financing of Terrorism (CFT) Cell" 
has been established in the Minist ry of Home Affairs since 2011 to 
coordinate with various intelligence an d enforcement agencies to prevent 
financing of terrorism. 
 A Terror Funding and Fake Curre ncy Cell (TFFC) has also been 
established in the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to investigate and 
prosecute terrorist funding and Fake Indian Currency Notes (FICN) cases. 
 A FICN Co-ordination Centre (FCORD) is also functioning to share the 
intelligence/information amongst the different security agencies of Centre 
and States to counter the circulation of FICN within the country. 
 Various sanctions have been imposed against terrorist organizations and 
its members through United Nati ons Security Council Resolutions 
(UNSCRs) 1367, 1373 and Section 51  (A) of the Unlawful Activities 
(Prevention) Act, 1967 which includes freezing, seizing and attaching 
funds/properties, thus restricting flowin g of funds of terrorist entities and 
travel restrictions on the members of a terrorist organization and 
designated individual terrorists. 
 Two Multi-Disciplinary Groups were form ed in Ministry of Home Affairs in 
2016 to monitor the flow of funds to LWE cadres; one at Centre Level and 
another at State level.  
 For effective choking of funds and ot her resources to LWE, coordinated 
actions are being undertaken by State Police in conjunction with Central 
agencies. These actions include plugging the systemic loopholes, ensuring 
coordination among various agencies, including sharing of information and 
actions to block the funding channel an d initiate legal action, monitoring 
progress of cases under investigation/prosecution, identifying various

modus operandi being employed by the financial conduits with a view to 
evolve counter measures etc.   
 The NIA has been substantially strengthened and the State Investigation 
Agencies (SIA) have also been estab lished in LWE affected States. Four 
NIA Special Courts have been operationalised in Chhattisgarh and efforts 
are also underway to establish exclusive courts in other states. LWE 
related UAPA cases are being monitore d through IMoT portal to facilitate 
the agencies in investigation, prosecution and monitoring. 
(ii)  On development front, apart from th e flagship schemes of Government of India 
(GoI), several LWE affected areas specific initiatives have been taken with special 
thrust on expansion of road network, improving telecommunication connectivity, 
education, skill development and financial in clusion. A few of these are enumerated 
below: 
• For expansion of road network, 15,016  km have been constructed under 02 
LWE specific schemes namely Road Requirement Plan (RRP) and Road 
Connectivity Project for LWE Affected Areas (RCPLWEA). 
• For improving telecom connectivity in LW E affected areas 9,233 towers have 
been commissioned.  
• For Skill Development, 46 Industrial Training Institute (ITI) and 49 Skill 
Development Centres (SDC) have been opened. 
• For quality education in tribal areas 179 Eklavya Model Residential Schools 
(EMRS) have been made functional.  
• For financial inclusion, Department of  Posts has opened 6,025 Post Offices 
with banking services in LWE affected di stricts. 1804 Bank Branches and 1321 
ATMs have been opened in Most LWE affected districts.  
• For further impetus to development, funds are provided for filling critical gaps in 
public infrastructure in Most LWE a ffected Districts under Special Central 
Assistance (SCA) scheme. Till now, Rs . 3,953.67 crore have been released 
since the inception of Scheme in 2017. ( iii)  The resolute implementation of the 
‘National Policy and Action Plan 2015’ has resulted in consistent decline in 
violence and constriction of geographi cal spread.  LWE which has been a 
serious challenge to the internal security  of the nation has been significantly 
curbed in the recent times and has been constricted to only a few pockets. The 
number of LWE-affected districts redu ced from 126 in 2018 to only 08in 
December-2025 with only 3 districts now remaining Most LWE Affected.

Need for a Dedicated National Response for Type 1 Diabetes in India 
DR. ANIL SUKHDEORAO BONDE (Maharashtra) : Sir, there is an urgent need for a 
dedicated national framework to support children and young adults living with Type-1 
Diabetes, a lifelong autoimmune condition th at strikes early and demands daily insulin 
and vigilant care. Unlike Type-2 diabetes, Type-1 is not lifestyle-related and cannot 
be prevented. It requires round-the-clo ck access to insulin, glucometers, ketone 
strips, trained providers and school safety protocols. India has over 1 million people 
living with Type-1 Diabetes, yet their needs ar e not fully integrated into public health 
programmes. Since they do not fall under the ‘rare’ disease category and are 
relatively small in number, they are of ten overlooked in NCD (Non-Communicable 
Diseases) programmes. Meeting their need s is neither complex nor unaffordable. 
India already manufactures world-class insulin used globally.   
I, therefore, urge the Government to: firs tly, create a national Type-1 Diabetes 
pathway with dedicated budgets; secondly, ensure uninterrupted access to insulin 
and monitoring tools across public facilities;  thirdly, mandate school safety protocols 
for hypoglycemia management; fourthly, strengthen device regulation and data 
systems for better care outcomes. Type 1 Di abetes care is an opportunity to save 
lives, uphold health equity and make India a global leader in compassionate and high 
quality diabetes care.

Demand for operationalization of South Coast Railway (SCOR) Zone 
SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I bring to the notice of 
the Government the long-pending issue of operationalising the South Coast Railway 
Zone with its headquarters at Visakhapat nam, as assured under the Andhra Pradesh 
Reorganisation framework. The new railway zone was envisaged to correct regional 
imbalances, improve administrative effici ency and accelerate rail way infrastructure 
development in Andhra Pradesh.                                                            
 Although some preliminary steps have b een taken, including the initiation of 
staff transfers from South Central Railway, the South Coast Railway Zone is yet to 
become fully functional. The absence of a formal Gazette Notification, independent 
budgetary allocation and full administrati ve autonomy has delayed the expected 
benefits. As a result, important decisions related to railway expansion, passenger 
facilities, freight movement and project execution continue to face avoidable 
procedural delays. Operationalising SCoRZ is crucial for improving rail connectivity 
across coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema, enhancing freight handling for 
ports and industrial corridors and strengthening passenger services in fast-growing 
urban regions. A functional Zone will also support port-led development, industrial 
growth and employment generation, especially in port cities and backward districts. 
Sir, I urge the Union Government to expedite the issuance of the formal 
Gazette Notification, provide adequate budgetary support, ensure full administrative 
and operational independence, and clearly outline a time-bound roadmap for making 
the South Coast Railway Zone fully operational.  
Timely action is essential to honour commitments made to the people of 
Andhra Pradesh and to strengthen regional rail infrastructure in line with national 
development goals. Thank you, Sir.

Demand for dialysis facilities in the rural and semi-urban areas of Tamil Nadu 
DR. M. DHANAPAL (Tamil Nadu) : Sir, I draw attention of the Government to the 
serious inadequacy of dialysis facilities for Chronic Kidney Disease patients in the rural 
and semi-urban areas of Tamil Nadu. Ch ronic Kidney Disease has emerged as a 
major public health concern, particularly affecting economically weaker sections who 
are unable to access or afford regular dialys is. While the efforts to  introduce dialysis 
units at select government hospitals have  been made, a recent assessment of 
Primary Health Centres and peripheral health institutions reveals significant gaps in 
dialysis infrastructure, availability of tr ained nephrology technicians, nurses, and 
proper maintenance of dialysis machines. In many centres, services are either non-
functional or severely under-utilised due to  manpower shortages and lack of regular 
consumables. Patients from rural areas are compelled to travel long distances to 
district headquarters or private facilities, resulting in high out-of-pocket expenditure, 
treatment discontinuation and avoidable loss of life. 
I urge the Government to make comprehensive assessment of dialysis 
infrastructure, manpower deployment, and maintenance mechanisms at the primary 
and secondary healthcare levels in Tamil Nadu. Government should also expand 
affordable and decentralised dialysis se rvices at the primary healthcare level, 
particularly through public-private partners hips, mobile dialysis units, and enhanced 
central assistance under national health sc hemes, so that life-saving dialysis care 
becomes accessible to the poorest and most vulnerable sections of society.

MR. CHAIRMAN:  Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the passing away of 
Shri Thomas Kuthiravatto m, a former Member of this House, on the 12th  of January, 
2026, at the age of 80 years. He served as  a Member of the Rajy a Sabha representing 
the State of Kerala, from April, 1985 to April, 1991. 
  Born on the 1st  of June, 1945, at Kallissery in Chengannur, Kerala, Shri Thomas 
Kuthiravattom began his public  life through student and youth movements and steadily 
rose to occupy important positions in Kerala’s political landscape. Known for his 
simplicity, commitment to public service, and concern for the poor and downtrodden, 
Shri Thomas Kuthiravattom was widely respect ed across political and social circles in 
Kerala. 
  In the passing away of Shri Thomas  Kuthiravattom, the country has lost a 
dedicated social worker and an able Parliamentarian. 
  I request Members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed.

state:

(b)     if so, whether any steps have been taken to address this issue; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI ARJUN 
RAM MEGHWAL): (a) to(c) A statement is laid on the Table of the House.                                
                                                              Statement 
(a) to (c) Pendency of cases in courts arise due to several factors which inter 
alia, include complexity of the facts involv ed, nature of evidence, co-operation of 
stakeholders, viz., bar, investigation agenci es, witness and litigants, the availability of 
physical infrastructure, supporting court staff, etc. besides the shortage of judges. The 
disposal of cases is within the exclusive do main of the judiciary. However, the Central 
Government is committed for speedy disposal  of cases and reducing pendency as 
mandated under Article 21 of the Constitu tion and has taken several initiatives to 
provide an ecosystem for faster disposal of cases by the judiciary. 
i. The Government has been filling up vacanci es of Judges in the Supreme Court of 
India and the High Courts from time to time. From 01.05.2014 to 19.01.2026, 72 
Judges have been appointed in the Supreme Court. 1162 new Judges were 
appointed and 820 Additional Judges were  made permanent in the High Courts 
during the same period. The sanctioned strength of Judges of the High Courts 
has increased from 906 in May, 2014 to 1122 till date.  Further, filling up of vacant 
positions of the judicial officers in Di strict and Subordinate courts is the 
responsibility of the High Courts and State Governments concerned. As per the 
Constitutional framework, in exercise of  powers conferred under the proviso to 
Article 309 read with Articles 233 and 234 of the Constitution, the respective State 
Government, in consultation with the High Court, frames the rules and regulations 
regarding the appointment and recruitmen t of Judicial Officers.  The Hon’ble 
Supreme Court vide order passed in Ja nuary 2007 in the Malik Mazhar Sultan 
case, has inter-alia stipulated certain ti melines, which are to be followed by the 
States and the respective High Courts fo r recruitment of judges in District and 
Subordinate Courts. 
ii. The National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms was set up in August, 
2011, with the twin objectives of increasing access to justice by reducing delays in 
the system and enhancing accountability through structural changes and by 
setting performance standards and capacities. 
iii. Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of Infrastructure

Facilities for District and Subordinate Courts, a sum of Rs. 12,461.28 crore has 
been released since the in ception of this Scheme in 1993-94. The number of 
Court halls has increased from 15,818 (as on 30.06.2014) to 22,683 (as on 
31.12.2025) and the number of residential units has increased from 10,211 (as on 
30.06.2014) to 20,029 (as on 31.12.2025), under this Scheme. 
iv. The Phase-III of the eCourts Project (2023-2027) approved on 13.09.2023 with an 
outlay of Rs.7,210 crore to make justi ce delivery progressively more robust, easy 
and accessible. As on November, 2025, 618.36 crores pages of court records 
have been digitized in the High Courts an d District Courts. More than 3.89 crore 
hearings have taken place through Vide o conferencing and live streaming is 
functional in 11 High Courts. The numbe r of eSewa Kendras (facilitation centres) 
has increased to 2059 across High Courts and District Courts. 
v. Arrears Committees have been set up in a ll 25 High Courts and the District Courts 
as well to clear cases pending for more than five years.   
vi. Fast Track Courts have been established for expeditious trial of specific 
categories of cases including heinous cr imes, cases involving women, children, 
persons with disabilities, individuals afflic ted with terminal illnesses, and property 
related cases pending for more than five years. As per information received from 
the High Courts, 876 FTCs are functional across 21 States/UTs as on 30.11.2025. 
Further, ten Special Courts are functional in nine (9) States/UTs for expeditious 
trial and disposal of criminal cases involving elected MPs / MLAs.  
vii. Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme namely Fast Track Special Courts 
(FTSCs) Scheme, 774 Fast  Track Special Courts (FTSCs) including 398 
exclusive POCSO (ePOCSO) Courts are fu nctional across 29 States/UTs as on 
30.11.2025, for the expeditious disposal of pending cases of Rape and POCSO 
Act. 
viii. The Government has also amended The Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) 
Act, 2018, The Commercial Courts (Ame ndment) Act, 2018, The Specific Relief 
(Amendment) Act, 2018, The Arbitratio n and Conciliation (Amendment) Act, 
2019 and The Criminal Laws (Amendment ) Act, 2018 with a view to reduce 
pendency.  
ix. Alternate Dispute Resolution methods have been promoted. The Commercial 
Courts Act, 2015 was amended in August , 2018 making Pre-institution Mediation 
and Settlement (PIMS) mandatory in cas e of commercial disputes. Amendment 
to the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 has been made by the Arbitration and

x. Lok Adalat is an important Alternative Disputes Resolution Mechanism available to 
common people, where the disputes/ cases pending in the court of law or at pre-
litigation stage are settled/ compromised amicably.   Under The Legal Services 
Authorities (LSA) Act, 1987, an award made  by a Lok Adalat is  deemed to be a 
decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all parties and no appeal lies

(a) to (d) The Conference Cl earance System (CCS) portal 
(conference.epolclearance.gov.in) is an  automated, single -window web- based 
application developed by the Ministry of External Affairs in March 2025 to streamline the 
process for granting political clearance to foreign nationals to attend or participate in 
conferences/seminars/workshops/ sports events and other events organised in India 
by government or private bodies.  
 This digital platform has ensured a smoother and hassle-free user experience 
with a substantial reduction in processing ti me as compared to the earlier mechanism. 
The portal also serves the la rger objective of Digital Indi a by maximizing the number of 
services available on the digital platform. 
 The portal serves as a cen tralised platform where stakeholders can access all 
the information related to the status of an  application in one place. It features an 
interactive dashboard that enables the Ministry to seek missing or additional information 
from organisers promptly, whenever required. Organisers can also monitor the status 
of their applications online. These features have substantially reduced the average 
processing time by at least five to six working days.  
 In general, political clearance is gran ted within 3-5 working days. However, the 
actual processing time may vary on a case-to -case basis depending on several factors 
including the number of invitees – which ma y range from 10 to 200 and the countries

Demand for construction of flyover or underground passage to protect elephant and 
wildlife corridors in the foothill areas of North Bengal 
SHRI NAGENDRA RAY (West Bengal): Sir, I would like to bring to your notice that 
the corridor from Russia to Africa via China, Myanmar, Bharat, Bhutan, Nepal, 
Pakistan, Afghanistan, Iran, Iraq, Jordan and Israel is the longest corridor in the 
world. Out of this stretch, Alipurduar to S iliguri is the main corridor covering national 
sanctuaries like Jaldapara-Chilapata, Garuma ra National Park, Baikunthapur forest, 
Mahananda wildlife sanctuary used by elephants from era to era. The hill is situated to 
the north of this corridor and to the south is density of population. So, in between 
these areas, the main elephant corridor is situated. But, developmental activities like 
construction of railway tracks, national high ways, etc. have been gradually leading to 
the destruction of elephants and other animal s which is detrimental to the Wild Life 
Protection Act, 1972. It is very regrettable to say that 41  elephants have died on the 
168-kilometre long way from New Jalpaiguri  Junction to Alipurduar Junction since 
2004 and, furthermore, a large number of elephants, including calves, have died 
during the last few years. There are estima ted 488 elephants which have been facing 
serious threat from increasing growth of human population. India still holds population 
of around 27,000 elephants as per the Government of India data in 2017. North Bengal 
has a total of 3,306 square kilometres forest area, out of which 2,000 square 
kilometres is considered as elephant habita t. But, today, this corridor is congested 
and occupied by human beings.  I, ther efore, request the Union Government to 
construct either flyover or underpass for human beings without any disturbance to 
elephants and other animals for their free movement. Thank you.

SHRI HARSH MAHAJAN (Himachal Pradesh) :  Hon. Chairman, Sir, I would like to 
draw the attention of this House to the Pa ngi Valley region in Chamba district of

nation.  
[ 06 February, 2026 ]

Sir, Pangi Valley is a tribal-dominated area in the aspirational district of 
Chamba. It is home to more than 25,000 tribal citizens who remain cut-off from the 
rest of the country for nearly eight months every year. Due to poor and seasonal road 
connectivity, access to healthcare, ed ucation and essential services becomes 
severely restricted. Moreover, this region is  one of the most beautiful regions in the 
country and when connected will unlock a huge opportunity for tourism in the region 
and enhancing the social and economic potential of this region. The development of 
Chamba-Killar road into an all-weather ro ad, along with the proposed Chaini Pass 
Tunnel of about 8.5 kilometres, will end this isolation. Sir, this corridor also carries 
exceptional strategic importance. At present, NH-154A connects Pathankot to 
Chamba, and a seasonal road exists up to Killar. А missing link of about 52 kilometres 
towards Leh needs to be developed. Once completed, this route will become the 
shortest approach to Leh, reducing th e Pathankot-Leh distance from about 800 
kilometres to nearly 450 kilometres, and Pathankot-Kargil from 1,000 kilometres to 
around 550 kilometres. This corridor originates from Pathankot Cantonment, a major 
defence base, and passes through strategica lly-sensitive terrain close to both the 
LAC and the LOC. It will provide a vital al ternative to Manali-Leh axis, reduce single-
route dependency, and strengthen defence logistics, emergency mobilisation, and 
medical evacuation. Sir, this project perf ectly aligns tribal welfare, regional 
development, and national security. 
Sir, I urge the Government to kindly  declare Chamba-Killar-Leh corridor as a 
strategic defence route and entrust it s development to the Border Roads 
Organisation, so that our border-prepare dness and our most-remote citizens are 
strengthened together. Thank you, Sir.

#*77. SHRI MAYANKKUMAR NAYAK : Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE AND 
FARMERS WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry has evaluated th e outcomes of digital agriculture 
initiatives  undertaken or continued in 2025, including AgriStack, Digital 
Crop Survey, Namo Drone Didi Scheme, Kisan e-Mitra and others; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including fa rmer coverage, integration with land 
records and improvements in access to  credit, insurance and real-time 
advisory services; 
(c) whether the Ministry has assessed the impact of these initiatives on 
productivity, income levels and market linkages for farmers; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, includin g coverage and measurable outcomes, 
State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE AND FARMERS WELFARE (SHRI SHIVRAJ 
SINGH CHOUHAN): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of House.  
Statement 
(a) to (d) Yes Sir, the Government co nsistently evaluates the outcomes of 
digital agriculture initiatives undertaken or continued during 2025. Some of the major 
initiatives are as under: 
I. AgriStack: The AgriStack is a Digital Pub lic Infrastructure (DPI) which 
consists of three foundational registries or databases associated with the 
agriculture sector, i.e., the Farmers Re gistry, Geo-Referenced Village Maps, 
and Crop Sown Registry, all creat ed and maintained by the State 
Governments/ Union Territories. It establishes a  single source of truth  for 
farmer identity, land, and their crops. 
 
Farmer ID enables seamless integration of Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) 
schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi Yojna (P M Kisan), 
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojna (P MFBY), Minimum Support Price (MSP) 
based procurement, access to credit deliv ery, input distribution, and disaster 
relief. As of 04.02.2026, more than 8.48 Crore Farmer IDs have been 
generated across the country.

Digital Crop Survey has enabled plot-level visibility of crops and better 
estimation of sowing patterns across seasons, which in turn supports 
evidence-based planning for procuremen t, input supply and logistics. In 
Kharif 2025, the Digital Crop Survey (DCS) has been conducted in 604 
Districts covering more than 28.5 crores plots across the country.  
Maharashtra has successfully  leveraged AgriStack for  scheme delivery, 
disaster relief, Artificial Intelligence (A I)-based advisory, and providing credit 
access, including the transfer of  over ₹14,000 crore to 89 lakh farmers for 
Kharif 2025 crop losses. Chhattisgarh has institutionalized Farmer ID and 
Digital Crop Survey for  MSP-based paddy procurement, covering  over 32 
lakh farmers  in a single season, significantly improving transparency, crop 
verification, and timeliness of MSP payments. 
II. Krishi Decision Support System: Krishi Decision Support System is a geo-
spatial platform that integrates satellite imagery, weather, soil, and crop data 
using Geographic Information System (GIS) to support agricultural planning 
and decision-making. This acts as an analytical platform (web-portal) for 
developing targeted advisories on crop, weather and soil.  
 
III. Kisan e-Mitra: It is a voice-based Artificial  Intelligence (AI)-powered chatbot 
developed to assist farmers with responses to their queries on the PM Kisan 
Samman Nidhi scheme. This solution su pports 11 regional languages and is 
evolving to assist with other government programs. At present, it handles 
over 8,000farmer queries on an average da ily and so far, more than 95 lakh 
queries have been answered. 
 
IV. National Pest Surveillance System: The National Pest Surveillance System, 
for tackling the loss of produce due to climate change, utilizes AI and 
Machine Learning to detect pest infest ation in crop issues, enabling timely 
intervention for healthier crops. This tool, currently used by over 10,000 
extension workers, allows farmers to ca pture images of pests to help them 
mitigate pest attacks and reduce crop losses. At present, it supports 65 
crops and over 400 pests.

reduced cost of operation and to empo wer SHGs as drone service providers 
for increasing their income and provid ing livelihood support. Lead Fertilizer

FELICITATIONS BY THE CHAIR 
Congratulation to the Indian Under-19 Cricket Team for winning the ICC Under-19 
Men's Cricket World Cup 
MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Members, it is with immense pride that I refer to the 
outstanding achievement of the Indian Under-19 Cricket Team in winning the ICC 
Under-19 Men's Cricket World Cup at Hara re, Zimbabwe, defeating England team by 
a commanding margin and bringing great honour to the nation. This remarkable 
effort, which is a record extending Sixth Under-19 World Cup title, once again 
highlights the depth of talent, commitment and sporting excellence among our youth. 
Hon. Members, I always applaud team work and while this success belongs to 
the entire team, I would also like to place on record, special appreciation for the 
young prodigy, Vaibhav Suryawanshi, who scored extraordinary 175 runs, the highest 
ever in the Under-19 Cricket World Cup Finals.  Brilliant individual performances by his 
colleagues in the run-up to the Final were truly inspiring and reflect the promise of a 
bright future. On my own behalf and on be half of this House, I extend heartiest 
congratulations to the captain, players, coaches and the entire support staff, and 
wish these young champions many more laurels in the years to come.

Concern over hardship arising from time limit on filing TDS correction statements 
SHRI SAT PAUL SHARMA  (Jammu and Kashmir) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, certain 
amendments were introduced by the Fina nce Act, 2024 to Section 200(3) of the 
Income Tax Act, 1961. These amen dments, effective from April 1 st, 2025, impose a 
six-year time limit for filing TDS correction statements calculated from the end of the 
financial year in which the original statement was required to be furnished.  
Sir, prior to this, there was no statutory time limit, allowing indefinite revisions 
for genuine errors like incorrect PAN details, challan mismatches or clerical mistakes. 
For TDS statements relating to financial ye ars prior to 2018-19, the six-year window 
had largely expired by March 31 st, 2025 in most of the cases.  As a result, corrections 
for this period became barred after that date aligning with the latest description of 
restrictions effective post-March 31 st, 2025. This has indeed led to reported 
hardships, including deductees not receiving proper TDS credit in Form 26AS 
12
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

resulting in inflated tax demands or de layed/refused refunds. As a result, the 
deductors are facing demand for short dedu ctions, interest penalties under Sections 
201 and 220, and the potential prosecution or  litigation, despite having deducted and 
deposited the tax correctly. Sir, these issu es can arise even when the tax was duly 
paid, as mismatches prevent proper credit allocation.   
Mr. Chairman, Sir, the suggestion for one-time relief/condonation window or 
guidelines under Section 119 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 is appropriate. Section 119 
empowers the CBDT to issue orders, instructions or directions to relax provisions in 
case of genuine hardships, including all cla sses of persons or income, while no such 
specific relief has been anno unced for pre-Financial Year 2018-19 periods. Similar 
condonation have already been  granted in the past for the TDS-related issues by the 
CBDT from time to time. Such relaxation can be given. I think it is viable. Thank you.

vendors, home-based workers, migrants, and gig workers. Despite their contribution 
of more than half of the national GDP, the vast majority remain outside any system of 
social protection. The Periodic Labour Forc e Survey and data indicate that less than 
10 per cent of unorganised workers have access to any form of social security benefit.

this settlement, Kerala was allocated 30 TM C of Cauvery water, including 6 TMC for 
the Bhavani basin, of which 2.87 TMC is specifically earmarked for Attappady. This 
allocation constitutes a settled legal right,  not a discretionary or negotiable claim. 
Despite this legal finality, the project continues to face procedural  delays. A scientific 
Environmental Impact Assessment is requir ed for environmental clearance, which in 
turn necessitates the issuance of Terms of Reference by the Ministry. Notably, the 
Expert Appraisal Committee identified no technical or ecological impediments. 
However, the proposal was returned citing the need for inter-State clearance.  I urge 
the Ministry for the prompt issuance of the Terms of Reference and statutory 
clearances, recognising Kerala’s legal mandate to utilise its allocated share from the 
Bhavani basin, which is essential to ensu re justice and development for the drought-

prone, predominantly tribal region of Attappady, while upholding environmental 
responsibility.  Thank you.

Chairman, Sir, I draw attention of the Government to the need of preserving 
brotherhood, unity and social harmony in our country. India’s strength lies in its 
diversity and the Constitutional values of  equality, fraternity and justice. Any

weakens our social fabric and must be firmly discouraged. I would also like to express

secure and equally valued in our great nation.

Concern over impact of air pollution on education 
DR. FAUZIA KHAN (Maharashtra): Thank you, Vice-Chairman, Sir, for giving me the 
opportunity. Sir, learning is impacted when  the air children breat he harms their ability 
to think, remember, and concentrate. In our country, it is the lived reality of millions of 
[ 09 February, 2026 ]
139

children. Evidence is clear, even aone -microgram rise in PM 2.5 reduces 
mathematics performance by up to 16 per centage points and reading by nearly 9 
points. Delhi’s pollution levels are consistent ly far above safe limits, and air pollution 
steadily erodes learning outcomes. Humans do not develop an immunity to polluted 
air. Our bodies do not adapt; lungs and brains suffer cumulative damage, causing 
poorer attention, memory, and school pe rformance. Sir, cleaner air improves 
learning, proving this loss is preventa ble. Yet our policy response remains 
fragmented. The National Education Policy fa ils to address how pollution and climate 
shocks disrupt schooling itself. The National  Action Plan on Climate Change does not 
treat education as a core pillar at all. In stead, we see reactive measures -- school 
closures, early holidays, online classes -- without long-term planning. There is no 
robust data on learning losses, no continuity plans for mid-day meals, and no serious 
investment in climate-resilient school infr astructure. Without institutional clarity and 
sustained investment, learning losses will co ntinue to undermine national progress. 
Sir, I urge the Government to look into it. Thank you.

Demand for tax exemption and enhanced support for National Bank for Agriculture 
and Rural Development (NABARD) 
SHRI K.R.N. RAJESHKUMAR (Tamil Nadu): Vanakkam, hon. Chairman, Sir. I rise 
today to draw the attention of this House and the Government to the critical role of the 
National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) and the urgent need 
to strengthen its financial autonomy and operational capacity. The NABARD is the 
backbone of our rural economy. It plays an important role in agricultural credit, rural 
infrastructure development, and helps in maintaining incomes across the nation. It is 
the true Mother Bird of our rural sector development and in supporting the very 
foundation of our nation's wealth. However, the financial framework, under which the 
NABARD operates, severely restricts its ability to fulfil its mandate. The imposition of 
taxes on NABARD's operations drains resources that should directly uplift rural 
communities. I urge the Government to remove Income Tax imposed on NABARD.  
Additionally, the allocation for the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), 
managed by the NABARD, must be substantially increased. The RIDF is crucial for 
rural infrastructure, market access and irrigation, yet its current allocation is 
inadequate. Moreover, the RIDF resources must be exclusively directed towards 
[ 10 February,2026, ]
25

agricultural and rural development. While MSMEs, NHB and SIDBI are important, 
their funding should not come at NABARD's expense. The NABARD needs higher 
budgetary support, greater autonomy and investments in technology and human 
resources to fulfil its mission effectively. Sir, I urge the Government to remove 
NABARD's income tax burden, increase the RIDF allocation and empower NABARD 
to drive rural wealth. Strengthening NABARD means strengthening our nation. Thank 
you, Sir.

Need for constitutional clarity on the definition and identification of minority 
communities in the country 
SHRI PAKA VENKATA SATYANARAYANA (Andhra Pradesh) : Thank you,               
Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. I wish to draw the attention of this 
august House to an important constitutional policy issue - identification of minorities. 
As and when India attained independence, certain communities had been said to be 
categorized as minorities. Today, after more than seven decades, their number has 
doubled, which can influence so many constitutional bodies in this system of electoral 
reforms.  Originally, the backward classes which were said to be under the category 
of nomadic, semi-nomadic and denotified tribes, which had been very weaker 
sections, which were numerically very less in number and also very less in income, 
which had minimum needs for their daily livelihoods, they were kept under the 
categories of backward classes and other weaker sections. They are the original 
minorities as per the recent statistics and as has been prescribed in the Constitution 
either through their numbers or through their language or through their habitations or 
whatsoever it may be. I would urge the Government, through you, Sir, to once again 
recall the original concept of minority, under what category it comes, what the 
importance of minority is, how it can be defined and what the sections are that can be 
conferred under the minority groups. Once again it has to be examined by the 
concerned Ministry, so that the original backward classes people, who were originally 
weakened by the system, can become strong; policy of social justice can be 
implemented as per the intention of Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar; and as per the 
intention of Antyodaya, the members who are originally marginalized can have an 
equal status through their upliftment and we can have Viksit Bharat. I urge the 
Government, through you, Sir, to look into it.  Thank you, Sir.

Demand to increase pension under National Social Assistance Programme to elderly 
people Below Poverty Line (BPL) 
SHRI GOLLA BABURAO (Andhra Pradesh) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, through you, I want 
to bring to the notice of the august House a very sorrowful issue that is going on in our 
country. It is an appeal to increase the pension under National Social Assistance 
Programme to elder BPL people. Social care is a crucial part of any Government to 
provide much-needed support to old people who need assistance for their survival 
and daily needs. The old age pension scheme is a significant step toward fulfilment of 
the Directive Principles of State Policy which mandates the Government to undertake 
welfare measures. No doubt, the Government of India is implementing its schemes. It 
is one of the five sub-schemes of National Social Assistance Programme that 
provides monthly pension to BPL senior citizens. But the most unfortunate part is that 
the Government of India is providing just Rs. 200 per month as pension to BPL senior 
citizens of the country. The second painful fact is that the current system of 
determining beneficiaries relies on antiquated methodology that fails to reflect 
present-day socio-economic realities; thereby, excluding a substantial number of 
genuinely eligible individuals. The third painful fact is that the Union Government has 
capped the number of beneficiaries from all States at 3 crore when the country has 
nearly 15 crore senior citizens.  The fourth painful fact is that the Budget for this has 
been stagnant since 2015-16. I am not saying that all 15 crore are eligible. But, as per 
estimates, around 5.1 crore elderly people are under BPL category. So, all those who 
are eligible should be provided financial assistance under the Government of India 
schemes. The Government of India is giving it to only 3 crore people, thereby 
depriving financial assistance to more than 2 crore people. The point is: Rs. 200 given 
by the Government of India is too low; it was last enhanced, more than one decade 
ago. So, there is an urgent need to increase the amount from Rs. 200 to, at least, Rs. 
1,000 per month. Thank you.

Need for bringing all hospitals in Puducherry under the ambit of Central Government 
Health Scheme (CGHS) 
SHRI S. SELVAGANABATHY (Puducherry) : Sir, today, I rise to draw the urgent 
attention of this august House to a matter of deep concern affecting our senior 
citizens – the Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) for pensioners as 
implemented in the Union Territory of Puducherry. The issue is that the CGHS was 
envisioned as a lifeline for retired Government servants, ensuring that their medical 
needs are met with dignity and efficiency. However, in Puducherry, the scheme 
currently covers only two empanelled hospitals though there are six medical colleges 
with hospitals. Even JIPMER, which is a Central Government institution, is not in the 
list! This severely restricts access for pensioners, many of whom are aged and frail. 
The present system requires pensioners to first obtain approval from a CGHS Centre 
and then seek treatment only in the approved list of hospitals. This bureaucratic 
process causes delay in medical care which is, particularly, burdensome for elderly 
patients. The serious human impact is this. Just imagine an aged pensioner in large 
cities like Chennai suffering from a sudden cardiac problem or requiring dialysis! 
Instead of going to the nearest hospital, they are forced to search for a CGHS Centre 
and navigate administrative hurdles. It is not just inconvenient; it is a matter of life and 
death. The very purpose of CGHS is defeated if access to timely treatment is 
compromised. Pensioners, who have dedicated their lives in service to the nation, 
should deserve seamless healthcare without procedural delay. The hospitals are not 
interested since the rates, in their opinion, are not remunerative. Further, the rates are 
not revised annually commensurate with the rise in the cost of maintenance. Another 
important reason is that the payments from CGHS are delayed due to procedural and 
administrative problems. The broader vision is that the healthcare is not a privilege; 
but it is a fundamental right. By strengthening CGHS in Puducherry, we would set a 
precedent for other regions where similar gaps exist.

Demand for restoration of the original 120 km jurisdiction of the Farakka Barrage 
Project Authority 
SHRI MOHAMMED NADIMUL HAQUE (West Bengal) : Sir, the Farakka Barrage is a 
Union project. It is controlled and operated by the Union Government. And yet, when 
West Bengal bears the devastating consequences of land erosion and siltation, the 
Union suddenly claims it has no responsibility. That is why the Farakka Barrage 
Project Authority’s full 120-Kilometre jurisdiction must be restored immediately.   
Sir, in 2005, the Union Government accepted a basic scientific reality that a 
river functions as a single system. Acting on this, it extended the Farakka’s 
jurisdiction to 40 Kilometres upstream and 80 Kilometres downstream. This decision 
was not political but hydrological. Sir, what changed in 2017 was the Union 
Government's willingness to bear responsibility, when Farakka's jurisdiction was cut 
down to 19.4 Kilometres. Erosion and siltation does not stop at notification 
boundaries. The Union made this position explicit in its letter dated 28 th July, 2022 
t
hat the barrage project authority is responsible only for the safety of the barrage. 
Erosion beyond 19.4 kilometers is the State's responsibility. At the same time, the 
Union retains complete control over barrage gates, and the silt regime. This is not 
federalism. This is the Union Government keeping power while exporting damage.

Need for examination reforms in view of rampant irregularities and paper leak 
SHRI A.D. SINGH (Bihar) : Mr. Chairman, Sir, I wish to raise the following matter of 
urgent public importance, ‘Need for examination reforms in view of rampant 
irregularities and paper leak.’ Sir, in recent years, the credibility of India's examination 
system has been severely undermined by repeated instances of irregularities and 
paper leaks in both Central and State-conducted recruitment and entrance 
examinations. These instances not only disrupt the lives of lakhs of aspirants, but also 
erode public trust in institutions meant to ensure fair and transparent selection 
processes. Several high-profile cases have come to light. The NEET-UG 2024 paper 
leak caused widespread protests across the country, raising serious questions about 
the security of question papers and the role of examination authorities. Similarly, in 
Bihar, the Bihar Public Service Commission (BPSC) and the Teacher Recruitment 
Exam have witnessed repeated paper leaks, leading to cancellations and arrests. In 
Rajasthan, the Rajasthan Eligibility Examination for Teachers (REET) has faced major 
controversies in multiple editions, with evidence of organized cheating racket involving 
officials and coaching centers. States like Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and 
Haryana have also faced similar problems in police, teachers and clerk-level 
recruitment exams. The core reasons behind such failure are lack of strong cyber 
security protocols, corruption within examination and printing agencies, outsourcing 
without proper checks and political interference. The absence of a standard for 
examination governance and inadequate use of technology further weakens the 
process. The Government has initiated some steps - the Public Examination 
(Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 which criminalizes organized cheating and 
recommends penalties, but only in Central sphere. However, more robust measures 
are needed which should also serve as model to States. This includes: Use of end-
to-end encrypted digital question paper delivery, deployment of AI-based surveillance 
in exam centers, Centralized regulations of private printing and logistic agencies, 
establishment of a National Examination Security Authority and holding top officials 
accountable for administrative lapses. Additionally, there is an urgent need for speedy 
trial of offenders, blacklisting of corrupt service providers and transparent grievance 
redressal system for affected candidates. In conclusion, examination reforms are 
critical not only for restoring student’s confidence, but also for safeguarding the 
merit-based recruitment foundation of India's governance and education system.  
Thank you, Sir.

Balagarh Project of Kolkata Port 
*106. SHRI SAMIK BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of PORTS, SHIPPING AND 
WATERWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a)  whether Government has approved and initiated implementation of the 
Balagarh Project of Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port, Kolkata for setting up a 
new cargo handling facility on Balagarh Island, about 85 km upstream from 
Kolkata; 
(b)   the objectives of the project, including decongestion of the Kolkata Dock 
System and improvement of inland waterway connectivity; 
42
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

(c)   the present status of land acquisition, environmental and other statutory 
clearances and tendering; 
(d)     the estimated project cost, funding pattern and timelines; and 
(e)  the proposed cargo handling capacity, trade benefits and employment 
potential envisaged upon commissioning? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PORTS, SHIPPING AND 
WATERWAYS (SHRI SHANTANU THAKUR): (a) to (e) A statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
 
Statement 
(a) Yes. 
(b) To accommodate anticipated traffic growth and reduce intra-city cargo 
movement, Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port Authority (SMPA) is developing dedicated 
container and coal berths at Balagarh.The project also seeks to promote cargo 
transportation through National Waterway-1, thereby, strengthening inland waterway 
connectivity and enhancing overall logistics efficiency. 
(c) Land is already available with the SMPA and environmental clearance 
was received on 24.01.2025. Under the Engineering Procurement and Construction 
(EPC) component of the project, the tender for road construction was opened on 
02.02.2026 and the work order for construction of the Road Over Bridge (ROB) has 
been issued on 09.01.2026. 
(d) The estimated cost of the project is ₹539.17 crore including the 
Engineering Procurement and Construction (EPC) component of Rs.131.97 crore and 
Public Private Partnership (PPP) component of ₹407.20 crore. The EPC component

Statement 
 (a) The Government is addressing malnutrition among women and children 
through Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, which includes Poshan 
Abhiyaan, Anganwadi Services and the Scheme for Adolescent Girls, and is 
implemented through Anganwadi Centres across the country, including Madhya 
Pradesh.Under Mission Poshan 2.0, a new strategy has been made for reduction in 
malnutrition and for improved health, wellness and immunity through activities like 
community engagement, outreach, behavioural change and advocacy.Ayush 
healthcare has been given due emphasize in Poshan 2.0 through anganwadi centers 
with a  focus on prevention of diseases and promotion of wellness through Yoga, 
cultivation of medicinal herbs in Poshan Vatikas, and preparation of Ayush 
formulations to address conditions like anaemia. 
 As part of these efforts, 31,709 Poshan Vatikas have been developed in 
Anganwadi Centres in Madhya Pradesh, while more than 3.13 lakh Poshan Vatikas 
have been developed across the country. The Ministry of Ayush participated in 
Poshan Maah and Poshan Pakhwada organized by the Ministry of Women and Child 
Development (MWCD) through its National Ayush Mission (NAM), National 
Institutes, Research Councils and Ayush Colleges across the country, during which 
more than four crore Ayush-based activities were conducted nationwide from 2021-
2025. 
 The Suposhit Gram Panchayat Abhiyaan under Mission Saksham Anganwadi 
and Poshan 2.0 of MWCDlaunched on 26 December 2024, incentivises top 
performing Gram Panchayats to strengthen Anganwadi services and nutrition related

activities with a focus on measurable improvements in nutritional outcomes of 
children, pregnant women and lactating mothers. However there is no specific 
initiative titled Suposhit Bharat. 
 (b) Yes, under NAM, the service delivery framework of Ayush Health and 
Wellness Centres, now known as Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (Ayush), envisages 
care during pregnancy and childbirth as one of its activities through preventive 
pregnancy care (Garbhini Charya), including appropriate food and lifestyle practices 
for the woman and family, specific dietary preparations, use of home remedies, and 
Yoga. 
 Further Supraja program (Ayush Maternal and Neonatal Intervention) under 
NAM is a specialized initiative aimed at promoting maternal and neonatal health 
outcomes by integrating Ayush-based preventive, promotive, and therapeutic care 
into existing public health systems. 
 (c) Yes, as per the data received from Directorate of Ayush, Government of 
Madhya Pradesh immunity-boosting kits were distributed to vulnerable populations in 
all 51 districts of Madhya Pradesh, including 20 tribal districts. The kits contained 
AYUSH-64 and other immunity-boosting Ayush medicines, such as Ayush Kadha, 
TrikatuChurna, Sanshamani Vati, Anu Taila, Arsenicum Album and 
KhameeraMarwareed. The details are enclosed as Annexure. 
 Also the Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS), an 
autonomous organization under Ministry of Ayush is providing Ayurveda Health care 
services in tribal dominant areas across the country at the door steps, through the 
Tribal Health Care Research Programme (THCRP) under the Development Action 
Plan for Scheduled Tribes (DAPST) through 14 CCRAS institutes in 14 states, 
including Madhya Pradesh state. Under this programme, Ayuraksha Kits containing 
Chyawanprash, Ayush Kwatha, Samshamani Vati, and Anu Taila were distributed by 
the CCRAS-Regional Ayurveda Research Institute (RARI), Gwalior, in Scheduled 
Tribe-dominated areas of Chhindwara district, specifically Block Tamia, Madhya 
Pradesh, during the financial year 2021-22.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Now, Q. No. 109. 
Benefits of U-Win Portal 
#*109. SHRI MITHLESH KUMAR : Will the MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a)  the total number of children and pregnant women registered on the U-WIN 
portal; 
(b) whether QR code vaccination certificates were issued for every vaccine 
dose in 2025; 
(c)   if so, the total number of such certificates issued; 
(d)  the number of SMS reminder messages sent to people in rural areas about 
upcoming vaccine doses; 
(e) whether U-WIN helped identify children who had never received any 
vaccine; and 
(f)  if so, the number of such “zero-dose” children who were brought under 
vaccination? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY  
WELFARE (SHRIMATI ANUPRIYA PATEL): (a) to (f) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House.  
Statement  
  (a) As on 3 rd February 2026, 11.05 crore children and 3.75 crore pregnant 
women are registered on U-WIN portal. 
 (b) and (c) Every beneficiary can download the QR code based vaccination 
certificate from U-WIN portal. In the year 2025, 8.01 crore beneficiaries were 
registered in U-WIN and the digital QR code based certificates were made available to 
them. 
 (d) A total of 29.42 crore SMSs including reminder SMSs were sent to 
beneficiaries in 2025 from U-WIN portal.

over Rs 18 lakh crore within a massive budget of Rs 53.47 lakh crore exposes the true 
financial condition of the country. How the Government portrays a Budget with a 24 
percent deficit as "excellent" is beyond the imagination of the common man. As an 
Odia, I will not hesitate to say that this Budget has brought great disappointment to 
the people of Odisha. Like 4.5 crore Odias, I too hoped that the 'double engine' 
Government would deliver for the state. It was expected that the Government would 
emphasize on infrastructure, employment opportunities, and additional grants to 
accelerate Odisha's progress. However, I must say with regret that the Union Budget 
has been a complete letdown for Odisha. 
The Budget includes Odisha in the National Waterways Project. Ironically, this 
proposal is a decade old. In 2008, six waterways in Odisha were included in National 
Waterways-5, yet not a single one has been implemented to date. Re-introducing it 
now is like a new cover to a old book. While Odisha’s rivers are gasping on 
"deathbeds" of sand due to the negligence of neighboring states, the Finance 
Minister’s dream of sailing ships on dry sand is like rubbing salt into the wounds of the 
Odia people. Odisha has also been included in the Rare Earth Corridor. But how will 
Odisha benefit? This corridor will merely facilitate the extraction and easy 
transportation of mineral resources—coal, iron ore, bauxite, and chromite—out of 
the State. The people of Odisha will be left with nothing but dust, smoke and 
pollution. Given that coal royalties have not been revised for years and the Centre 
maintains an inconsistent policy on green tax, there is no reason to believe this will 
benefit Odisha in any way. 
Sir, the budget announced seven High-Speed Railway Corridors, yet Odisha 
did not receive a single one. Not even one corridor will pass through the State. 
Furthermore, Odisha has been neglected in the Buddhist Circuit Development Plan. 
Ratnagiri, Udayagiri, and Lalitgiri—known as the "Diamond Triangle" of Buddhist 
tourism—have been completely ignored.  While the Government announced support 
for handlooms and Khadi, the GST on handicrafts and handlooms—the lifeline for 
lakhs of weavers in Odisha—has not been reduced. Additionally, Odisha finds no 
place in the development plan for 200 industrial clusters. When the BJP came to 
power in 2014, it promised Special Category Status for Odisha. Yet, even after 12 
years, the Central Government remains silent; the issue is not even mentioned in this 
budget. The repeated demand for a disaster-resilient ecosystem for Odisha, which 
92
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

faces regular natural calamities, has been ignored. The State has been completely 
deprived of proposed chemical parks, hi-tech tool rooms, eco-friendly freight 
corridors, container production units, and programs to enhance coconut and cashew 
production. 
Sir, the entire country was watching this Budget. However, the Finance 
Minister did not utter a single word for the common man during her 85-minute 
speech. The middle class hoping for income tax relief, the youth seeking 
employment, and the common citizens praying for price reductions have all been 
deeply disappointed. While the 2025-26 Budget seemed tailored for the Bihar 
elections, many now feel this Budget is focused on the upcoming elections in West 
Bengal, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu. In a federal system, the development of the state 
should be the priority for the nation's growth; unfortunately, the "Development of the 
East" (Purvodaya) appears to be confined only to speeches. Thank you, Sir.”

giving me the opportunity to speak on the Union Budget 2026-27.

Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, the Budget, 2026-27 is anti-youth, anti-farmers, 
anti-women and anti-workers. I can only say that this Budget will bring rural distress 
and unemployment of unimaginable levels. Sir, the border and hill districts across the 
country have been facing high levels of unemployment among the youth, but the 
Budget document has not envisaged any roadmap for addressing the concern of 
these areas. I have my own doubt that the youth of that sensitive area may be lured 
by the hostile neighbouring countries against the interests of the nation. 
Sir, I will not dwell upon the issue of core importance, that is, conflict in the 
naxalism-affected areas and Kashmir, as many learned speakers have spoken about 
poor allocation in the Budget for the same. Being the lone Opposition voice from the 
North-East Region in this August House, I would like to highlight the false promises 
made to the people of the North-East. The promises ring hollow when immediate 
concerns remain unaddressed. Assam is yet to receive Rs. 27,000 crore from the 
Centre for flood and disaster management. In a State where floods are a yearly 
headache and thereby roads deteriorate rapidly, the Budget has just remained silent 
and the people of Assam have been left to their destiny to face river bank erosion, 
which displaces lakhs of vulnerable and poor people.  Sir, with barely two months left

SHRIMATI JEBI MATHER HISHAM (Kerala) : Sir, I thank my Party for giving me the 
opportunity to speak on the Budget. On the 1 st of February, 2026, on a freezing 
Sunday morning, we waited with high expectations, the nation waited in hope, the 
stock exchange kept fingers crossed. Three days before, the Economic Survey was 
tabled with key challenges in it. We expected, the nation expected, the stock 
exchange expected that the identified challenges in the Economic Survey would be 
addressed by the Finance Minister in her Budget Speech.Then came the much-
awaited moment. We heard Madam Finance Minister speak for 85 minutes; 15,623 
words were spoken. We heard words like first kartavya, second kartavya, third 
kartavya, sankalp, yuvashakti, viksit Bharat, fiscal prudence. We heard phrases like 
‘action over ambivalence’, ‘reform over rhetoric’, ‘people over populism’, 
atmanirbharta. But, Sir, we did not hear Economic Survey 2025-26. Nation did not 
hear challenges outlined in the Economic Survey. We saw stock market crashing, 
stooping all time low, immediately after the Finance Minister's Budget Speech.  
Nation did not hear about the capital investment, unemployment issue, issue of slow 
growth rate or slow fiscal consolidation. We heard, the nation heard all of these issues 
which were outlined in the Economic Survey, from the hon. former Finance Minister.  
Shri P. Chidambaram spoke at length about these issues. Randeep Surjewala ji 
brought to light in detail false announcements versus media hype, the reality of zero 
allotment and zero spending, the fund cuts in crucial sectors and how the rural poor 
and poor farmers stand ignored in this Budget. Neeraj Dangi ji highlighted the play of

numbers in this Budget, how the youth, the SCs/STs, laborers stand ignored in this 
Budget.  
Sir, I want to add a few concerns. The Budget was presented on 1 st of 
February. On 2nd February, in the midnight hours, when India was sleeping, President 
Trump announced to the world the US-India trade deal. President Trump dictated 
India to lower trade barriers, to stop purchase of Russian oil, to buy oil from US and 
Venezuela. President Trump did a shout-out. Prime Minister Modi also committed to 
buying more than 500 billion US dollars worth of US energy, technology, agricultural 
and other products -- all in the midnight hour, Sir. We remember the words of our 
first Prime Minister, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, spoken at the midnight in the Tryst with 
Destiny. “At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake                                                  
to    life    and    freedom.” And now, it is ‘tyrst with destiny’.* 
 And after the whole world came to know, our Prime Minister tweeted. I quote, 
“Wonderful to speak with my dear friend President Trump. Delighted that Made in 
India products will now have a reduced tariff of 18 per cent. Big thanks to President 
Trump on behalf of 1 billion people of India for this wonderful announcement." Sir, 
please note, the word ‘wonderful’ was used twice in one tweet. *I respectfully ask 
the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister: Is it really wonderful? Is it really 
wonderful to lower the trade barriers to the US? Is it really wonderful to surrender our 
freedom to decide from whom we should buy oil? Is it really wonderful to give a 
whopping commitment of 500 billion dollars worth of US energy, technology, 
agriculture and other products? Will it be really wonderful for our farmers? I 
respectfully ask the Prime Minister, ‘Is it really wonderful to have 6 th February Order by 
the US President which says that Washington will establish a US Monitoring 
Committee tasked with overseeing India's implementation of the oil prohibition and 
violation?’ I respectfully ask the Prime Minister, ‘Isn't this US Monitoring Committee 
mechanism kick-starting precedence for foreign oversight of India's policy 
decisions?’ I respectfully ask the Prime Minister, ‘Isn't this marking the beginning of a 
rare instance of American oversight on India's energy sourcing decisions and clear 
attack on India's sovereignty?’ Are we a rogue nation to be monitored? I respectfully 
ask the Prime Minister, ‘Isn’t this Presidential Order by your so-called ‘wonderful 
friend’ effectively surrendering India’s energy security to America’s Presidential 
whims?’ Our Prime Minister said ‘wonderful’ twice for this. The nation would like to 
know this. The nation has the right to know this.  Just as I remember Nehru ji, I also

Now let me speak about my home State, Kerala. The Union Budget once again 
has shown complete neglect towards Kerala. Kerala was expecting AIIMS. But there 
is no AIIMS. Kerala was expecting high speed rail. But there is no high speed rail.  No

expecting second development phase of Vizhinjam Port.  But there is no approval, no

rubber. Kerala was expecting special project to reduce the challenge of man-animal 
conflict and projects to counter agricultural loss. But there is nothing for that. Kerala 
was expecting project for modern paddy storage. But there is nothing for that.   
Wayanad MP Priyanka Gandhi ji has been continuously requesting for 
Wayanad. But request for Wayanad package still remains unfulfilled. Kerala was 
expecting Pravasi Rehabilitation. There is nothing for that. Kerala was expecting a 
Special Package of Rs.21,000 crore considering the loss caused to the GSDP and 
reduced borrowing limit. But there is nothing for that. And what did Kerala receive?  
Kerala received aamma, the sea turtle. Newspapers are a reflection of the mood of 
the State. See this, Sir. It is not atmanirbhar. It is aamma nirbhar. This I want to 
authenticate.

to the ecology, Kerala's fragile ecosystem and livelihood. Fisherfolk and coastal 
communities have concerns. Also, there is a concern whether this is exploitation to 
protect corporate interest masqueraded as policy. We often hear the Prime Minister, 
the Home Minister and the Finance Minister speaking about cooperative federalism.

SHRI MASTHAN RAO YADAV BEEDHA (Andhra Pradesh) : Thank you, Vice-
Chairman, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. On behalf of Telugu Desam party and 
our leader and Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister, hon. Nara Chandrababu Naidu, I rise 
to wholeheartedly support the Budget 2026-27. It reflects our commitment to 
achieving a Viksit Atmanirbhar Bharat  by 2047. There has been a clear increase in 
public capital expenditure from Rs. 2 lakh crore in 2014-15 to Rs. 12.2 lakh crore in 
the financial year 2026-27. This strong infrastructure push will have a definite GDP 
multiplier effect. The fiscal deficit is estimated at 4.3 per cent of GDP in 2026-27, 
down from 4.4 per cent in 2025-26. The debt-to-GDP ratio is estimated at 55.6 per 
cent in 2026-27, compared to 56.1 per cent in 2025- 26.                                                             
Tax on income has increased from Rs.14,38,000/- crores to Rs.14,66,000/- crores, 
indicating a sense of confidence people have in the Government. These figures show 
that the NDA Government is balancing national growth with fiscal responsibility. This 
Budget strengthens India's economic foundation towards growth, inviting confidence 
in our future.  
Respected Vice-Chairman, Sir, as regards development and infrastructure, 
the proposed high-speed rail corridors linking Hyderabad-Bengaluru and Hyderabad-
Chennai will significantly improve logistics efficiency. Districts such as Anantapur, 
Kurnool and Nellore in Andhra Pradesh will benefit from faster freight mobility. This will 
support industry, agriculture and regional value chains. The continued emphasis on 
the East Coast Industrial Corridor is timely. I request the Government to consider a 
dedicated East Coast Freight Corridor linking major port cities in my Andhra Pradesh 
State, including Visakhapatnam, Kakinada, and Nellore. This will integrate coastal 
manufacturing clusters with the national and global supply chains. I also thank the 
Government for taking up the Dugarajapatnam Port in Andhra Pradesh under the Ship 
building Development Scheme.   
Now, I come to fisheries and marine economy. Sir, Andhra Pradesh remains 
India's leading fish and shrimp producing and exporting State. Recent trade 
developments, including tariff rationalization with the USA and the EU provide relief to 
aqua farmers and exporters. I thank the Government for making fish catch by Indian 
fishing vessels in the Exclusive Economic Zones and on the High Seas duty-free. This 
will encourage fishermen to explore beyond traditional waters and expand marine 
productivity. Under the PM Matsya Sampada Yojana, projects worth over Rs. 2,400/- 
crore have been sanctioned in Andhra Pradesh with substantial Central support.  
While implementation is underway, I urge a faster execution, so that infrastructure, 
cold chain and processing facilities translate into higher farmer incomes. I also 
114
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

request enhanced access to modern deep-sea fishing vessels and integrated supply 
chain facilities.  
Sir, as regards skill development and technology, this is the year of futuristic 
technology in India. From hosting the AI summit to promoting adoption of AI and 
blockchain, our country is leading technological change. Under the leadership of Sri 
Nara Chandrababu Naidu Garu and hon. Prime Minister Narendra Modi ji, Andhra 
Pradesh is once again emerging as a technology hub. Our State has captured over 25 
per cent of proposed investments in the first nine months of financial year 2026 and is 
a front-runner in attracting large-scale capital. Major hyper scale data centre 
proposals in Vishakhapatnam, close to US $ 25 billion investments have transformed 
the city into a major capital infrastructure hub. A Quantum Valley is being developed in 
Amaravati, Andhra Pradesh's capital, to boost India's global standing in next 
generation computing. Renewable energy sites and green hydrogen plants are being 
established to reduce carbon emissions and attract sustainable investments. 
However, specialized training is required. 
 Then, I come to Defence and strategic manufacturing. India's Defence 
production has surpassed Rs.1.5 lakh crores. Defence exports have crossed Rs. 
23,000/- crores. Andhra Pradesh, with its ports and industrial corridors, is well 
placed to host ancillary Defence manufacturing and logistics infrastructure. 
Sir, lastly, Andhra Pradesh has rich Buddhist heritage sites such as Amaravati, 
Addurru and Nagarjunakonda. Structured investment in Buddhist tourism 
infrastructure will generate employment and strengthen cultural engagement. In 
conclusion, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, this Budget combines macroeconomic stability, 
infrastructure-led growth, technological transformation and social inclusion. With 
cooperative federalism and focussed implementation, Andhra Pradesh can accelerate 
its journey towards Swarna Andhra Pradesh while contributing to the national Vision of 
Viksit Bharat. I thank the hon. Finance Minister for having given us a good Budget and 
good allocation to Andhra Pradesh, particularly. I extend my full support to the Union 
Budget 2026-27. Jai Andhra, Jai Viksit Bharat. Thank you, Sir. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (DR. DINESH SHARMA) : Next is, Dr. Kavita Patidar; not 
present. Dr. Fauzia Khan; four minutes.  
DR. FAUZIA KHAN (Maharashtra) : Sir, we stand today at decisive crossroads. 
India's much-debated demographic dividend rests not in abstract numbers, but in the 
165 million children below the age of six, children who will constitute our future 
[ 10 February,2026, ]
115

workforce. It is the bedrock of India's human capital and non-negotiable for a long-
term economic growth. I would like to ask the hon. Finance Minister – she is not here 
but I would like to ask her -- whether we can really build a Viksit Bharat without first 
securing the rights of our youngest non-voting citizens. ECD must be seen as a 
fundamental human right because over 85 per cent of brain development happens 
before the age of six. If we miss this critical window, no later intervention can fully 
compensate for whatever is lost. What we failed to build in the early years, we spend 
a lifetime trying to repair it. It is precisely this neglect of our earliest foundations that is 
now reflected in our weak human development outcomes.  
Sir, our poor Human Development Index stands well, well below the world 
average. Progress cannot be measured only through infrastructure or by doubling the 
number of schemes. We must look honestly at what our HDI tells us. The WCD 
Budget for 2026-27 is projected at Rs. 28,000 crores, yet child-focused expenditure, 
as a share of the Union Budget, has fallen by 1 per cent from 2017-18, while the total 
spending on children remains below 1 per cent of GDP, far short of the 5 per cent 
recommendation by the National Plan of Action for Children. Despite the NEP-2020, 
40 per cent of rural children aged three to six remain outside preschools or 
anganwadis. 
 Sir, Japan has produced a disciplined and innovative workforce because 
Japan's universal access to kindergartens and nurseries has 90 per cent attendance, 
strong subsidies and zero waiting lists. Sir, Singapore has a similar focus. We are 
held back by weak utilization and fragmentation. We do not lack resources. We have 
Rs. 3.5 lakh crores in cess funds lying dormant, including 45 per cent of construction 
cess unspent. Sir, 30 million children require protection, yet the funding remains 
skewed and siloed. We cannot limp. We cannot afford to limp. We will miss the bus. 
Sir, the vision of India in 2047 risks becoming an India strong on paper, hollow 
at the core. I urge three reforms. First, we need to establish dedicated child 
budgeting units across Ministries to end silos and enable integrated-planning. 
Second, we need to move to outcome-based budgeting. Without age and gender-
disaggregated data, today, we are flying blind. Third, there should be a national pre-
primary education policy; a national board for pre-primary education, investing in the 
appointment of specially-trained staff in anganwadis with expertise in foundational 
learning. We have to invest in this because a child born at this very moment will be a 
21-year-old citizen in 2047.

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI BHUBANESWAR KALITA) : Hon. Members, the 
discussion on General Budget, 2026-27 will continue tomorrow. Now, we will take up 
the permitted list of Special Mentions.  The first Special Mention is of hon. Member, 
Shri Lahar Singh Siroya, on ‘Demand for protecting cultural livelihoods by integrating 
'Crafts Villages.’
 
SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Demand for protecting cultural livelihoods by integrating 'Crafts Villages’ 
SHRI LAHAR SINGH SIROYA (Karnataka): Sir, I rise to submit matter concerning the 
need to integrate cultural preservation with highway infrastructure development, 
especially in Karnataka. The Bengaluru-Mysuru Expressway, a flagship project of the 
Central Government, has impacted thousands of artisans and small business owners 
in bypassed towns.  Iconic, globally recognized traditions like the G.I. Tag, 
Channapatna wooden toys, and regional culinary heritage are seeing business drop 
by as much as 70-80 per cent. As I have urged previously, the construction of world-
class roads must not unintentionally destroy the vibrant economic and cultural fabrics 
of our smaller towns. I had raised this issue earlier as a special mention on December 
19, 2022. However, the situation of our artisans remains largely unchanged. 
132
[ RAJYA SABHA ]

I, therefore, make an earnest request to the Union Minister for Road Transport 
and Highways and MSME to immediately implement the crafts village, i.e., the 
Shilpgrama type of concept, along the new corridors starting with the Bangalore-
Mysore Expressway. This requires two essential steps. 
One, mandate the identification and development of permanent high-visibility 
sites or suitable Government land adjacent to the new expressways to serve as a 
marketplace for local artisans and MSMEs. Two, provide a dedicated central 
mechanism for financial and infrastructure support to develop these villages into 
state-of-the-art hubs that safeguard the livelihood of our traditional craftsmen and 
advance our Prime Minister's Vocal for Local vision. 
We must ensure modern connectivity also secures the future of our unique 
cultural heritage. I urge the Government to look into it.

Need for a responsible and forward-looking approach for Agniveers’ transition to 
civilian life 
SHRI I.S. INBADURAI (Tamil Nadu) : Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I rise to address the 
Government on the future of our Agniveers, particularly the first batch recruited under 
the Agnipath scheme, of which around 40,000 young Agniveers are expected to 
complete their four-year tenure and exit the Armed Forces in 2026. These young 
citizens joined the forces at a very early age and served the nation with dedication, 
discipline, and pride. The Government fully recognizes its responsibility towards 
them, not just during service, but equally after their exit. 
As per the scheme, up to 25 per cent of each batch will be given the 
opportunity for permanent enrolment in the Armed Forces based on merit and 
performance. The remaining 75 per cent will transition to civilian life with a tax-free 
[ 10 February,2026, ]

Seva Nidhi package of about Rs. 11.71 lakh, providing them financial security at a 
crucial stage. 
The Government has taken comprehensive steps for their re-employment and 
reintegration. There is 10 percent reservation for ex-Agniveers in CAPF and the 
Ministry of Defence, along with age relaxation. Many states have extended similar 
benefits in police and public sector jobs. 
I urge the Government to ensure skill certificates, educational support through 
NIOS and IGNOU, access to credit for entrepreneurship, and a dedicated placement 
portal through inter-ministerial coordination for Agniveers, so as to ensure that their 
service to the nation becomes a strong foundation for a secure and dignified future.  
Thank you, Sir.
